extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, law students, and legal practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying legal standards for assessing patentability, validity, scope, rights, and remedies (novelty, inventive act, specification, claims, patent office procedure, assignment, infringement, damages, etc.). The page is an index/summary of doctrinal criteria from a patent law treatise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requisites
rubrics_metrics.description: PATENTABILITY, requisites to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts take judicial notice of want of patentability in some circumstances; patentability cannot be decided on demurrer except in clear cases. The invention must 'conform to the essential nature of an invention' (see related entries on novelty, inventive act, utility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: NOVELTY, defined; legal novelty vs intrinsic novelty; novelty involves identity and priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty must formerly have been absolute; legal novelty (essential to patentability) differs from intrinsic novelty. Intrinsic novelty shows discovery but is not essential to patentability. Novelty may be negatived by prior knowledge or use only by practical and complete knowledge; defendant must prove want of novelty beyond reasonable doubt. Novelty involves identity and priority and is distinct from infringement issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive act / inventive skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventive act and inventive skill distinguished from mere mechanical skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanical skill is not inventive skill; standard of mechanical skill has been constantly raised and is to be estimated as it existed at date of alleged invention. Inventive act creates means and has particular nature and development; different inventions may accomplish the same end but identity is not proved by identity of end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility / Usefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility is relevant to patentability and as evidence of inventive skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utility and success with the public may evidence inventive skill; usefulness is treated in relation to novelty and patentability (useful inventions may be valid even for purposes not described).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims: scope, completeness, and construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim is 'the life of' the patent; claim completeness affects patent value and scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must be complete; excessive claims may render a patent defective. Claim language determines scope; courts construe patents liberally to sustain validity if possible. In combination claims, all claimed elements are essential. Value to patentee depends on completeness of claims; clerical errors and name errors have specific effects; claim identity must be preserved through amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification / Description sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Description/specification must adequately describe essential elements and not be ambiguous or fraudulent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A description incurably defective or omitting an essential element can render a patent invalid. Description must correspond with drawings and models; ambiguous descriptions make the patent invalid. Fraudulent misrepresentation in the specification can render a patent void and unamendable.

rubrics_metrics.name: New matter (re-issue constraints)
rubrics_metrics.description: NEW MATTER, defined; rule of properly applicable to re-issues; requires a new application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New matter cannot be introduced in re-issue—if new matter is involved a new application is required. Re-issue cannot cure certain wilful defects or false oaths; identity of patent must be preserved in amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority and date of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Priority involves identity and date; how priority is shown and evidence for priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oath to an application is prima facie evidence of priority. Date of invention and priority may be shown by evidence in Patent Office and courts; affidavits of third persons and other evidence of priority are admissible. Application filing dates and reduction to practice bear on priority disputes and interferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduction to practice as evidence of invention completion and priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing an application or a model does not by itself show reduction to practice. Reduction to practice is used as evidence in priority disputes and may be shown by other evidentiary means; courts examine whether the invention was completed at a given date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use / prior publication / anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior knowledge, prior public use, and prior publication can negate novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty is negatived by prior knowledge or use only when there has been practical and complete knowledge. Prior public use or publication can be a defense of want of novelty; careful proof is required (practical, complete knowledge).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Office examination and duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Functions, duties, powers, and limitations of the Patent Office and Commissioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Patent Office exists to secure correct and lawful letters-patent and has duty to see that claims are correct; rules of practice are statutory and the Commissioner has power to make rules. The Office cannot decide title questions, cannot repeal letters-patent, and has limited jurisdiction (e.g., no jurisdiction over abandoned patents). Proceedings in the Office are presumed regular; evidence and motions have specific procedures; appeals and new trials within the Office have defined rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Models for Patent Office
rubrics_metrics.description: Model requirements, sufficiency, and relation to specification/drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Models when required must correspond with the specification and drawings; models are not filed until ordered by the Commissioner. The sufficiency of a model is determined by the Commissioner; a model neither aids nor impairs the specification and drawings and does not in itself show reduction to practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function claiming ('means'/'mechanism')
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of 'means', 'mechanism', and similar words in claims when proper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Words like 'means' and 'mechanism' are permissible in claims when appropriate; there are rules about their use (e.g., in claims for combinations) and their consequences for claim scope and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination claims and essential elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims for combinations make all claimed elements essential; relationship to improvements and prior patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent for a combination treats claimed elements as essential; improvements cannot claim what is already covered by a prior patent's original. A patent for part(s) of a previously patented whole may be valid while a combination of previously patented elements cannot claim those elements anew.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent as contract and nature of patent privilege
rubrics_metrics.description: PATENT as a contract between inventor and the public; PATENT PRIVILEGE defined as a lawful monopoly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent privilege is a derogation of common right and is measured by the claim. It is a contract granting a lawful monopoly for a limited period in exchange for disclosure. The nature, scope, and justification (public policy, reward, stimulus) of patent privilege are doctrinally significant; rights are created at issue of letters-patent and governed by statutes and Constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity presumption and evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent as prima facie evidence that prerequisites were fulfilled; weight of patent in litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent is prima facie evidence of patentability prerequisites having been met; judgments sustaining a patent increase the weight of that evidence but patents are not conclusive in courts. Re-issue or extension may affect evidentiary weight. Patent office records and correspondence may be admissible as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defenses to validity (prior patent, prior use, identity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defenses include lack of novelty, prior patent, prior use, double use, identity, and want of inventive act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendants may assert want of novelty, prior patents, prior public use, or that the asserted invention is identical to prior art. Proof standards are strict (practical & complete knowledge; beyond reasonable doubt in some contexts). Foreign patents and prior domestic patents raise particular rules (e.g., later patents construed not to cover earlier if possible).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue and amendment limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Limits on amending patents and re-issues; identity must be preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent may be amended in some respects, but cannot be amended to change the inventor or to cover matter beyond the identity of the original patent; if amendments would change the identity or add new matter a new application is required. Patents void and unamendable if the specification misrepresents or conceals with intent to deceive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term, expiration, and foreign term interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Term of a patent is fixed by statute; ways of determining term and effects of foreign patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent term should be stated in letters-patent and is fixed by statute not by grant wording. Expiration rules and interactions with foreign patent terms (how measured, when limited or not) are specified; substituted patents and design patents have separate treatments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignability and transfer of rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Rights to apply for and own patents are assignable; distinction between property in invention and monopoly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The right to apply is assignable at any stage of the inventive act; property in the invention is transferable like other property though the monopoly has statutory and natural limits. Transfer affects exercise of rights; assignment governed by Patent Law; oral contracts may be constrained by Statute of Frauds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement: application of law to facts and limits of 'use'
rubrics_metrics.description: Application of patent law to factual settings (jury questions) and limits on what constitutes 'use'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application of patent to facts is for the jury. 'Use' of a patented invention does not necessarily cover making or selling the invention; infringement analysis depends on claim construction and factual evidence of unauthorized practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages and profits estimation
rubrics_metrics.description: Items allowable in estimating profits and damages (market value, manufacturer's profit, marketing costs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manufacturer's profit may be an item in estimating profits. Market value (distinct from marketability or scalability) and marketing cost may be allowed in estimating profits; rules and examples govern what items are recoverable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licenses and royalties (voidness where infringement exists)
rubrics_metrics.description: Licenses and license fees in various contexts and limits (e.g., license fees for infringing use).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: License fees to use an invention that infringes a prior patent are void. Notes or payments given for void patents may be recoverable or not depending on circumstances; license and royalty disputes interact with validity defenses and equitable considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentees, entitlement, and status of inventors
rubrics_metrics.description: Who may be a patentee and how entitlement is determined (earliest conceiver, employees, representatives of deceased).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentees must be the earliest conceiver if diligent in reduction; employees of the Patent Office may not be patentees; patents may be granted to representatives of deceased inventors; legal title vests at grant; joint patentees have distinct rules and are not necessarily partners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel, laches, and Patent Office doctrines
rubrics_metrics.description: Estoppel doctrines as applied in Patent Office and courts; limitations on estoppel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doctrine of estoppel is applied in Patent Office proceedings; however, the Patent Office is not estopped to deny the validity of its own grant in certain contexts. Motions decided without appeal may be final; delays and errors in Office proceedings do not necessarily work abandonment of rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oath, false statements, and evidentiary consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Oath to application as prima facie evidence of priority; false oaths have serious consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An oath to an application is prima facie evidence of priority; if wilfully false it may not be curable by re-issue and can render a patent invalid. False or fraudulent statements in the prosecution or specification affect validity and may be grounds for invalidation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parol evidence and admissibility in patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Admissibility of parol evidence and other extrinsic evidence in patent litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parol evidence admissibility is discussed in patent cases; Patent Office records, correspondence, and files of third parties may be admissible as evidence on questions like priority and prosecution history.
